Week 5 Class Entry

This week, we learned:

  • How to choose an appropriate graph given a data question
  • How to create basic plots in R
  • How to create and format graphs using ggplot2

Basic histogram example

For the mtcars data, create basic histogram for mph with proper titles and axis labels.

hist(mtcars$mpg,main = "Distribution of Miles per Gallon", xlab = "Miles Per Gallon (mpg)")

ggplot2 example

Create the same histogram using ggplot2.

ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = mpg)) + geom_histogram() 
`stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value `binwidth`.

Now add features to the histogram

ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = mpg)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of MPG",
    x = "Miles per Gallon (mpg)",
    y = "Number of Cars"
  ) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean(mpg)), linetype = 2)
`stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value `binwidth`.

This dataset shows the different miles per gallon, cylinders, displacement, horsepower, rear axle ratio, weight, 1/4 mile time, engine, transmission, forward gears, and carburetors for 32 different car models. We can see the average miles per gallon is 20.09, horsepower is 146.7, and weight is 3.22. There appears to be no outliers in the dataset.

Step 2: Compare Groups with tapply()

tapply(mtcars$mpg, mtcars$cyl, mean)
       4        6        8 
26.66364 19.74286 15.10000 
tapply(mtcars$mpg, mtcars$am , mean)
       0        1 
17.14737 24.39231 
tapply(mtcars$hp, mtcars$cyl, mean)
        4         6         8 
 82.63636 122.28571 209.21429

We can see that with more cylinders, miles per gallon goes down. We can also see that manual transmission cars have higher miles per gallon. Lastly, we can see that the more cylinders a car has, the more horsepower it has.

Step 3: Create Basic R Graphs

hist(mtcars$mpg, main = "Miles per Gallon of Cars in mtcars", xlab = "Miles per Gallon", ylab = "Frequency", breaks = 32)
boxplot(mpg~cyl, data = mtcars, main = "Miles per Gallon by Number of Cylinders", xlab="Cylinders", ylab = "Miles per Gallon")
plot(mtcars$wt, mtcars$mpg, main = "Scatterplot of Weight vs Miles per Gallon", xlab="Weight", ylab="Miles per Gallon")

The histogram tells us there is a wide range of mpg for the cars. Most cars were within the 15-23 mpg range. The boxplot shows that 4 cylinders is most fuel efficient but has the highest variability. 6 and 8 cylinder cars show very consistent yet lower fuel efficiency. The scatterplot shows a negative linear relationship between weight and miles per gallon.

Step 4: Recreate a Graph with ggplot2

ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg)) + geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = lm) + labs(title = "Scatterplot of Weight vs Miles per Gallon", x = "Weight", y="Miles per Gallon")
`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

I added a trendline to the scatterplot of weight vs miles per gallon. I like this version than the original better. With the trendline, you can easily see the slope of the negative linear relationship between weight and miles per gallon. We can see that the relationship is not exponential or logarithmic, for example; it is linear.

Step 5: Week 5 Reflection

I feel more confident in creating graphs that actually have meaning and interpreting that data in the real world. I feel like I may need more practice in knowing which type of graph (bar chart, histogram, scatterplot etc) would be the most appropriate for a given problem. I found it interesting that manual cars have higher fuel efficiency than automatic cars. When I buy my first car, it may just be a manual!

Week 8 Entry - Compute and interpret tests and confidence intervals

1. Simulate the data

design_A <- c(42, 55, 38, 61, 47, 52, 44, 58, 49, 36, 63, 51)

design_B <- c(54, 62, 47, 68, 59, 51, 65, 57, 72, 48, 61, 56)

2. Explore the data

mean_A = mean(design_A)
sd_A = sd(design_A)

mean_B = mean(design_B)
sd_B = sd(design_B)

boxplot(design_A,design_B, main = "Website Design", names = c("Design A", "Design B"), ylab = "Purchase Amounts ($)")

We can see that Design B is more profitable for the online retailer. There are no outliers for Version A or B. The retailer should use Design B.

3. Hypothesis test: Is there evidence that the population mean purchase amounts differ between Design A and Design B?

  1. H0: muA = muB, Ha: muA != muB
t.test(design_A, design_B, alternative = "two.sided") 

    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  design_A and design_B
t = -2.5767, df = 21.712, p-value = 0.01732
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -15.647508  -1.685826
sample estimates:
mean of x mean of y 
 49.66667  58.33333

alpha = 0.05 pval = 0.017 pval < alpha. We reject the null hypothesis. There is sufficient evidence to conclude that there are differences between Design A and B.

4. Confidence interval: Use the output from your test to report a 95% confidence interval for the difference in mean purchase amounts between Design A and Design B.

According to the output of the two sample t test, the 95% confidence interval is (-15.6, -1.69). We are 95% confident that the mean purchase amount of design A is between 1.69 dollars and 15.6 dollars lower than design B. The confidence interval does not include zero. That means that we can confirm that there is a difference between the two designs. Since we can see in the side-by-side boxplot that Design B is more profitable than Design A, our confidence interval can confirm how much more profitable Design B is than Design A.

5. Reflect

The online retailer should invest more in design B because it is more profitable than design A. The online retailer should investigate why design A is worse than design B, and use that information to improve both designs and conduct more tests to get evermore profitable.

colnames(police) = c("Male", "Female")

Females are more likely to be lower rank than males. 76% of females are officers, while only 69% of males are officers. As rank increases, it is more likely that those positions are filled by males. The proportion switches at Sergeant, where now more males fill the positions.

The mean grade level among gamers seems to be pretty low, only about a 66%, which would be a D. Also, gamers sleep level is lower than the commonly known average of 8 hours by about 1.5 hours. Perhaps they are staying up late playing video games. Most gamers have a “Medium” stress level, and there are more “Low” stress levels than “High”. There are only about 100 Male gamers than Females, which shows that there are about equal Male and Female gamers. Also, the genre of games is about equal for Males and Females. Each genre has about equal number of Male and Female gamers. The mean grades for gender is also about equal. Females have only about less than 1 percent better grades than Males.

Step 3: Visualize the Data

ggplot(game, aes(x = grades)) + geom_histogram() + labs(title = "Histogram of Grades", x="Grades", y="Count")

There are about equal number of male and female gamers. There are some gamers that have no gender.

Males and Females seem to have equal distribution of grades. However, both genders have median scores in the 60th percentile, which is not a passing grade (assuming 70% is minimum reuiqred for passing the class)

ggplot(game, aes(addiction_score, grades)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method = lm) + labs(title="Addiction Score by Grades", x="Addiction Score", y="Grades")
`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

There seems to be a negative correlation between Addiction Score and Grades. The higher the addiction score, the lower the grades.

ggplot(game, aes(x = gender, fill = stress_level)) + geom_bar() + labs(title = "Stacked Bar Chart of Gender and Stress Level", x="Gender", y="Count")

There seems to be equal stress levels compared with gender. Most gamers have medium stress levels regardless of gender.

Step 4: Estimate a population mean or proportion

One sample t.test

What is the average grade among gamers?

t.test(game$grades, conf.level = 0.95)

 66.18078

With 95% confidence, we can conlcude that the mean grade score among gamers is between 65.7% and 66.7%. We can conclude that gamers do not have very high or passing grades.

Step 5: Test an association with chi-squared

Is there a significant association between gamer’s gender and favorite game genre?

table2 = table(game$gender, game$gaming_genre)

chisq.test(table2)

    Pearson's Chi-squared test

data:  table2
X-squared = 1.2005, df = 4, p-value = 0.878
ggplot(game, aes(x = gender, fill = gaming_genre)) + geom_bar(position = "fill")
round(prop.table(table2, 2),2)
        
         Casual  FPS  RPG
  Female   0.48 0.48 0.47
  Male     0.48 0.49 0.49
  Other    0.04 0.03 0.04

Given that pval (0.878) > alpha (0.05), we fail to reject the null hypothesis. We cannot conclude that there is a significant association between gender and gaming genre.This holds in the prop table. We can see that there is not much difference between gender and gaming genre. If there was, we would see a significant difference between the percentage of genre across gender.

Step 6: Model a relationship with linear regression

What is the association between study hours and grades among gamers?

ggplot(game, aes(study_hours, grades)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method = lm)
`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

       1 
127.5991

Every hour of study increases grades by about 6.4 points. An intercept of 31.1 means that if a student studied for no hours, they would receive a grade of 31.1. With an r value of .734, we can see that there is a moderately strong positive relationship between study hours and grades.R^2 of .54 means that approximately 54% of grades can be explained by study hours. The pval is smaller than alpha, therefore we can conclude that there is an association between study hours and grades. Modeling a prediction of 15 study hours, a gamer would receive a grade of 127.6%. Given the limitation that it may be impossible for a grade to be higher than 100% given the individual professor, there are some grades in this data set that are above 100%, so it’s not impossible to receive such a high score.

Step 7: Reflect on what you learned

I found it most interesting that there is not much of a difference in any comparison between male and female gamers. Instinctively, I imagined there would be must more male gamers than female gamers. This was not the case given the bar plot of gender across all gamers. There are only slightly more males than females. Also, in comparison among genres, I imagined that more males would play first-person shooters while females would play more casual games. Again, this was not true, given that there were a similar number of gamers between genders across every single gaming genre. Also, according to the side-by-side boxplot, we can see that grades are uniform across genders. I found it interesting that most gamers are receiving failing grades. The box plot shows that the median score among gamers was lower than a 70%, which is a C-minus. Perhaps gamers play video games more than take their studies seriously. As a gamer myself, I can attest to the fact that sometimes gaming gets in the way of studies. However, I make sure to get my work done before satisfying my gaming urges (for the most part). A limitation is that this data set is specifically about gamers, so I wonder what the difference would be between students who do not play games versus students who do play games. I strengthened my ability to create meaningful graphs that can help give insights into the data. I found it difficult to find a diversity of categorical variables in this data set, since most were quantitative.

Week 12 Entry - Passion Project 2

Step 1: Identify y and potential predictors

The variable I want to predict is grades. The potential predictors include:

  • study hours
  • gaming hours
  • sleep hours
  • attendance
  • device usage
  • addiction score

I intuitively believe that these predictors would have an impact on grades. I know for me personally, I need to study a lot, game a little, attend class regularly, limit my device usage, and not be addicted to video games in order to maintain a high GPA. Also, having worked with this data previously, I know that gender and gaming genre are not a very good predictors for grades.I plan on leaving these variables out of my analysis.

I find it interesting that males and females have about the same grades. This is true for gaming genre as well, no matter what gamers play they receive about the same grades. Interestingly, “High” stress level gamers have a much higher grade than “Low” stress gamers. Perhaps the more stressed a gamer is, the more time they devote to their studies, which produces a higher grade. Lower stress gamers are probably taking it easy and not worrying about grades, which means they aren’t taking their studies as seriously, and therefore receiving a far lower grade. Not surprisingly, study hours has a relatively high positive correlation with grades. The more you study, the better grade you get. Also, gaming hours has a negative correlation with grades. This also makes sense, the less you game, the better grade you get.

Multiple R-squared:  0.9091,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.9091 
F-statistic: 1.333e+04 on 6 and 7993 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16

Assuming an alpha of 0.05, study hours, gaming hours, sleep hours, attendance, and addiction score all seem to be significant in this model.

Step 4: Model Improvement

I want to take out device usage, since this variable does not seem to have a significant association with grades with a very large p value. There could be an argument to leave in addiction score, given that it was slightly lower than alpha = 0.05. However, if we use a stricter alpha of 0.01, addiction score becomes obsolete, so let’s take that out as well. Study hours, gaming hours, sleep hours, and attendance have incredibly small p values and seem to be very good predictors of grades.

mod_final = lm(grades ~ study_hours + gaming_hours + sleep_hours + attendance, data = game)
summary(mod_final)

    attendance, data = game)

  • intercept: when all else is held at 0, grade is a 6.22, which doesn’t have a very practical meanin (all else equal)
  • study_hours: for every 1 hour of study, grade increases by 6.33 points (all else equal).
  • gaming_hours: for every 1 hour of gaming, grade decreases by 5.26 points (all else equal).
  • sleep_hours: for every 1 hour of sleep, grade increases by 3.79 points (all else equal)
  • attendance: for every 1 addition percent of attendance, grades increase by 0.28 points (all else equal)

Adjusted R^2 value is 0.909. That means that these variables can explain 90.9% of the variation of grade point averages (all else equal).

This final model explains most of the data, and every variable is statistically significant with incredibly low p values. I would say that this model is highly effective at describing grades using various variables.

new = data.frame(study_hours = 10, gaming_hours = 10, sleep_hours = 9, attendance = 95)
predict(mod_final, newdata = new)
       1 
77.59735

If a gamer studied for 10 hours, gamed for 10 hours, slept for 9 hours, and attended 95% of classes, their grade would be predicted to be a 77.6%.

Step 5: Interaction Term

I want to test the interaction effect of study hours and gaming hours has on grades.

ggplot(game, aes(x = study_hours, y = gaming_hours)) + geom_smooth(method="lm")
`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'
mod_final2 = lm(grades ~ study_hours + gaming_hours + sleep_hours + attendance + study_hours*gaming_hours, data = game)
summary(mod_final2)

Taking out device usage and addiction score, and adding the interaction effect, our coefficients change. We can see that as study hours increases, gaming hours decreases, which makes sense since there are only 24 hours in a day with a limited amount of time to allot to any 1 activity. According the the p value, the interaction effect of study hours and gaming hours is statistically significant at the 0.01 alpha level. I picked these two variables because of the opportunity cost of choosing one, the other, and both. 1 hour of studying offsets 1 hour of gaming by about 0.391 grade points.
